Quantity discount (menu pricing, but for different quantity)
(1) price for LQ equal to low WTP, (2) price for HQ that makes high type indifferent, (3) Check if price is higher if selling only high or low quantity
When more units, P has to incorporate CS to the first unit
Condition: seller wants to sell larger Q to the high type

PRICE DISCRIMINATION
Charge different prices not due to cost differences
Goal: capture consumer surplus and eliminate deadweight loss
First-degree (perfect): Each consumer charged WTP. Rare in practice, requires perfect information
Third-degree (segment/group): Groups face different prices (ex: students, seniors, geography, business).
Conditions: 1) Different buyers have different WTP; 2) Ability to identify who has high/low WTP; 3) Ability to segment buyers with different WTP.
Restrictions: Arbitrage, legal
Second-degree (menu): offering different versions of a product to introduce lower/higher value buyers to reveal themselves
Downside: Not perfect (CS and DWL - has to give value to consumers)
Advantage: no arbitrage and no need to identify/segment market
Versioning (ex: Freemium - Spotify) - quality

When I joined Egon Zehnder (EZ), their services had a single price across all clients. We soon realized that smaller companies, like startups, could not afford the full fee asked, while listed clients were less sensitive to price changes. To address this, we introduced third-degree pricing discrimination based on company size and segment. Startups and digital firms paid lower fees, while large listed companies paid more. This allowed EZ to win projects with elastic clients, while capturing additional revenue from less price-sensitive ones.

At Egon Zehnder, we faced challenges with third-degree price discrimination when clients compared fees and realized they were being charged different prices. To address this, we introduced a “menu of services” that allowed clients to self-select the option that best matched their willingness to pay. Instead of offering only the “full recruiting project” at a high fee, we created a new product: “strategic introductions.” In this model, we presented only the top five candidates we had interviewed and limited the level of market mapping. Although both services had similar marginal costs, they were framed differently to appeal to distinct client segments.

This is an example of versioning in second-degree price discrimination. It was profitable because the "high type” clients, such as large corporations, had a higher willingness to pay for the upgrade (comprehensive service), while "low type” clients, like startups, started to work with us as they could now afford the lower-priced version. Clients revealed their willingness to pay during early discussions by selecting between packages, allowing us to expand our customer base and increase revenue without openly charging different prices for the same service.
